03

The Chord Sequence

Watch at 0:43

All the examples will be in the key of
F major
.

Make sure you get this scale really secure in both hands before moving on—use the video to help you.

Here is the chord sequence we’re going to use for all the licks and fills we’ll be looking at.

Now, let’s add some rhythm to the chord sequence by breaking up the notes in our right hand using a
‘toggle’ pattern.

This chord sequence uses inversions to create smooth
transitions between the chords. If you want to incorporate
inversions into your playing, a full 25-page PDF lesson book is
available that guides you through every step of the process.

04

Lick #1: Simple...
But Effective!

Watch at 3:01

In this lick, we’re simply running down the notes in the F major scale, from the 4th to the root
(Bb, A, G, and F).

We’ll place this pattern on beat 4 of each bar we’re playing. Notice how we’re playing the F major scale
over all the chords—this is called “referencing” the key, and it helps glue everything together.

05

Lick #2: Triad Time

Watch at 5.03

Here, we’re going to use a triad shape in our right hand and again, this fill will come on beat 4.

This one is a bit trickier, as we need to hold down two notes in our thumb and little finger, then our
second finger is going to move, as demonstrated in the video. In other videos on the channel, this has
been referred to as a ‘
split triad
’.

This fill works well in the middle of the piano but also sounds great in a higher register to add
brightness and sparkle to your playing.

06

Lick #3: A Series Of Bells

Watch at 6:43

This fill uses a few more notes from the F major scale—we’re going to incorporate the root, the 5th,
and the 7th from the scale.

It sounds like a cascade of bells chiming, and again, we’re placing this fill on beat 4 at the end of every
bar.

07

Lick #4: The Semitone Clash

Watch at 9:34

This fill uses a triad shape with a semitone at the top—a really beautiful chord shape that I use all the
time in my playing.

Make sure you’re hearing the subdivision clearly in your head as you play it.

Try bringing this fill down an octave to reduce the jump between the main chords and the fill.

08

Lick #5: 6th Intervals

Watch at 11:01

This fill uses a sixth interval (with six notes between the bottom and top notes, including both).

The fingering can be a bit tricky—check out the video to see my approach!

Remember, every fill is based on the sound of the key— F major. This helps glue everything together,
making the chord progression feel cohesive and less jumpy. Using fills within the overall key grounds
the music, creating a smoother flow.

09

Lick #6: Adele?!

Watch at 12:43

This fill is inspired by classic piano ballads and is the most complex one we’ve explored so far, mainly
due to its syncopated rhythm and the cluster shape at the top.

Really focus on the rhythm here, making sure you’re subdividing in your head. This is the kind of fill you
could use in the final chorus, driving the song toward a powerful finish.

08

How To Create Your Own...

Watch at 14:35

To create your own piano fills and licks, begin by using the pentatonic scale of the key the song is in.

F major pentatonic

Go through your chord sequence and start improvising with notes from this scale to create your own
fills. Try to think of each fill as a ‘little melody.’

One way to approach this is by first coming up with a rhythm, then improvising the notes to match it.
Alternatively,
you
could
reverse
the
process:
plan
which
notes
you’ll
use,
but
freely
improvise
the
rhythm.

Incorporating licks and fills into your playing is the key to bringing flow and
fluidity to your chord sequences. Adding these ‘connectors’ between chords
instantly transforms your playing from blocky to free and flowing.

Work through all the licks in this book, and try playing them along with the
backing tracks. Experiment with putting them in different keys and inserting
them into the songs you’re working on. Most importantly—don’t be afraid to
create your own fills! That’s where the real fun begins.
